Project 9 · Research results · New model development

Project 9 Research: Every Model We Tested

The research phase in one place: what each model tried, what $10,000 would have become, and what we learned. Every test uses real bid/ask prices and fees, keeps each position within 5% of the account, retrains the model each year and judges it only on years it never saw.

Major goal: grow the account more than 5% a trading day after all costs, with +1% and +2% a day as milestones. That is far beyond anything tested so far, so progress is measured on a ladder of realistic steps: first beat the simple Elastic Net benchmark (L0), then +0.05% a day (L1), +0.10% (L2) and +0.25% (L3).

Status: 16 experiments · positions now 5% of the account (charter v1.9) · Experiment 9 reaches L2 in development, with ~50% drops Started Nov 6, 2026 Last updated Nov 8, 2026 · 17 experiments

In plain words

What works so far: a simple linear model (Elastic Net) that buys short-dated SPY/QQQ calls on days it scores well: $10,000 → $51,946 over 2016–2025 at 5% per position (worst drop about −35%). It mostly captures the market’s upward drift.

What we tried: six new transformer designs, intraday trading, single stocks, market timing and selling option premium. Until Experiment 9, none beat it on return and risk together.

First milestone: monthly put spreads run together with Elastic Net beat it on return and risk ($203,352, Sharpe 1.04 vs 0.68), and the spreads stayed profitable on fresh 2026 data. The win came from trading less often and combining unrelated edges.

Bigger positions (Nov 8): each position is now 5% of the account instead of 0.5% (up to 50% at risk). Every gain and loss is 10× larger, so steady strategies grow much faster — Experiment 9 reaches +0.12% a day (L2) — while volatile ones (most single-stock models) are wiped out. Results before Nov 8 were run at 0.5% and are restated here by scaling (approximate).

What holds us back: the bid/ask spread. Most option edges we can find in daily data are about as large as the cost of trading them, so the next rounds trade less often and look for slower, larger edges.

Top 10 models so far

Updated Nov 10, 2026. The first table is the new standard saved-file Top 10 (final); the second is the same models on QuantConnect’s standard test. Below it, the earlier two tables, one per trustworthy data source, so models are only compared with others tested on the same kind of data. Within each table, models are ranked by average daily account growth at 5% of the account per position, after costs, on their walk-forward test years (years they had not seen). Those two tables are pre-standard and kept as records: they will be replaced after every experiment is redone on the saved SPY/QQQ/IWM file and the new Top 10 is re-run on the QuantConnect standard test (see Next). Rows marked “approx.” are computed from month-end account values. Data names the exact source.

Top 10 — Saved SPY/QQQ file (daily) standard v1.3 final

Updated Nov 10, 2026 from every saved-file redo so far (1-F, 1D-2-F, 3-F, 4-F, 5-F, 7-F, 8-F, 9-F, 11-F) and Experiment 23. All tested on 2014–2025, SPY and QQQ only, learners trained from SPY 2010 / QQQ 2012, 5% per position, ask/bid + $0.65. Ranked by daily growth; duplicate accounts shown once. Final: families C (stock call picking) and E (graph networks) are not redone while the test uses only SPY and QQQ (owner, Nov 10) — they were built to rank many stocks; their results stay below as pre-standard records. The steadiest account, the charter put spread alone (Exp. 9-F: $34,602, Sharpe 0.80, worst drop −26%), ranks below #10 on growth. Nov 10 (owner): Experiment 50’s Kelly account with a daily 50% cap is #1, Experiment 43’s three-layer VVIX account #2, Experiment 39’s VVIX version #3, Experiment 36’s Fed tightening switch #4, Experiment 41’s VVIX + Fed/CPI event filter #5, Experiment 45’s SpreadGuard account #6, Experiment 43’s fearful-days-only account #7 and Experiment 31’s IncomeStack #8 (owner, Nov 10–11) and Experiment 30’s accounts #9–#10; the lowest-growth accounts moved off the ranked list; the Elastic Net benchmark stays listed unnumbered (it defines L0).

Steady growth (goal 4): S1 = at least 8 of 12 months up in every test year and no losing year; S2 = at least 10 of 12 months up every year and no month worse than −5%; S3 = every month positive. “Years meet S1” counts test years with 8+ months up and no loss; “misses” lists each failing year and why (fewer than 8 months up, a losing year, or both) — a year can be profitable and still miss S1 if fewer than 8 months were up; worst month = the largest one-month fall of the account at 5% per position. Growth steps: L0 beat Elastic Net (Sharpe above 0.68 and more daily return), L1 +0.05% a day, L2 +0.10%, L3 +0.25%, G1 +1% and +2%, goal more than +5%. (dev) = development walk-forward years, not yet confirmed on fresh data at 5% sizing. Worst drop from monthly values (exact daily for #1). $ per position = the range of dollars put into one position over the test years (5% of the account as it grew or shrank from $10,000; for spreads, the maximum possible loss). Holding time = trading days from opening to closing a trade. Return each test year = the account’s gain or loss in that calendar year at 5% per position (from month-end values). 2025 only = calendar 2025 alone for an account holding $10,000 on 1 Jan 2025 at 5% per position. Max open at once = the most positions held at the same time during 2025 (each 5% of the account). Mixed account = two strategies in one account; their 2025 per-trade results are shown separately (Elastic Net per trade on the option price over 1 day; spreads on the maximum possible loss over about a month). Experiments run at 0.5% are restated at 5% (each period’s result ×10, compounded).

Summary

Saved SPY/QQQ/IWM file: six of the ten sell a loss-capped put spread next to the Elastic Net call/put model (Experiments 8, 9 and 11: #1–5 and #9), and #8 is the put spread alone. It is the only family that reaches L1–L2 over ten years with roughly three months up in four. The Elastic Net benchmark is #7.

QuantConnect: at real 2 PM quotes the Elastic Net leg loses, so the combined accounts drop out; what remains are the put spreads on their own (#3, #5–7, #9: modest growth, the steadiest months) and monthly stock calls (#1, #2, #4: faster but with drops of 63–74%). Nothing on either table is above L3 (+0.25% a day): G1 (+1% a day) is 8× and the goal (+5% a day) 40× the best result.

Steady growth (goal 4)

No model reaches S1 (at least 8 of 12 months up in every year, no losing year) yet. Saved file: closest is #3, the transformer gate — no losing year in 2016–2025 and at least 8 of 12 months up in 9 of the 10 years; only 2022 (5 of 12) misses. QuantConnect: closest is the gated 0.25-delta put spread (#6) — 99 of 120 months up and a worst drop of only −18%.

Caveat: choosing the best of 80+ models flatters the winners, and drops are deep at 5% positions — every candidate needs a fresh-data check (paper trading or new months). Experiment 13’s momentum calls (formerly #4) used saved DoltHub data and are left out until redone.

Progress of every model

All results at 5% of the account per position (charter v1.9, Nov 8, 2026; earlier runs used 0.5% and are restated by scaling each period’s gain or loss 10× — an approximation; the exact daily recalculation for Experiment 9 gives $229,900 instead of $203,352). Log scale. Each bar shows what $10,000 became with one model on its test years, after costs (test periods differ by experiment; see the table), followed by its average net return per trade on the money put into each trade (for spreads: on the maximum possible loss). Combined accounts mix several strategies, so they show no per-trade figure. Right of the dashed line = made money.

Every model at a glance

Grouped by experiment, in the order they were built. Under “$10,000 →”, “months up” = how many calendar months of the test years ended with the account higher than it started the month (e.g. 89/120); the 2025 column shows the same count for 2025 alone (e.g. 8/12). Each test year shows its return from the start to the end of that year and, after the arrow, the approximate account value at the end of the year; positions are a percentage of the account at entry (e.g. 5%), so they grow with it. In the 2025 column, the dollar figure is the 2025 gain or loss on the account as it stood at the start of 2025. Per trade = average net return on the money put into each trade (spreads: on the maximum possible loss); trades = number of trades in the test years; win rate = share of trades that made money after costs; combined accounts mix several strategies (“mixed”); data = whether the model used end-of-day (daily) or intraday option quotes; “2025 only” = net profit or loss in dollars over calendar 2025 for an account holding $10,000 at the start of 2025, with the same as a percentage of the account (after all costs, at the official position sizes) and, in brackets, the range of dollars put into each position during 2025 (5% of the account, so it moves with the account’s value; for spreads, the maximum possible loss), then per trade, trades and win rate for trades opened in 2025, the last evaluated year (“not tested” = the model’s test ended before 2025). Sharpe = return per unit of risk (higher is smoother); L0 needs more than 0.68 together with more return than Elastic Net. * includes interest on idle cash; 0.68 without it.

Model and idea
learning over the years (edge over baseline)		Test years$10,000 →
months up / months
return each test year		All test years
per trade · trades · win rate		2025 only
net $ on $10,000 (%) · net % of $500 (5% of the account) · months up in 2025 · ($ invested per position) · per trade · trades · win rate		DataSharpeVerdictWhat it taught

Return each test year = the account’s gain or loss in that calendar year at 5% per position, from the month-end values behind each experiment’s chart (about monthly for the intraday experiments 16–19). Shown wherever a chart exists. Learning over the years (under each model): models are retrained every year on all earlier data, so later test years use more training history. Each year we compare the model with a simple baseline in the same experiment and year (random picks where available, otherwise the experiment’s rule or untrained version, named in each row): edge = how much faster the model’s account grew than the baseline’s that year, (1 + model) ÷ (1 + baseline) − 1, averaged over the years. This removes most of the effect of good or bad markets. The line compares the average edge in the first half of the test years with the second half: ↗ grew by more than 5 points, ↘ shrank by more than 5 points, → about the same. Where a baseline collapsed (e.g. random picks losing almost everything), the edge is shown as “over +100%”. Rules and random picks are not trained.

By strategy family

The same experiments grouped by trading method, so each method can be compared across data sources. Nothing is renumbered: every experiment keeps its number, and redos will appear as -F (redone on the saved SPY/QQQ/IWM file) and -Q (QuantConnect standard test, Top 10 only) in the same family. Each row shows the experiment’s pre-set main model in that family where there is one, otherwise its best model (random and other baselines excluded), with its verdict: what $10,000 became at 5% per position, with its Sharpe. All results so far are pre-standard.

Current loop: experiment by experiment (newest first)

Since Nov 7, 2026 the research runs as a loop: learn from every model and from outside research, design a new model, write its test plan before running it, test it on unseen years, publish the result here and record why it worked or not. After rounds without progress, the view of the problem changes (trade type, horizon, instruments), not just the model. Newest first.

Before the loop · Experiments 1–2Reference

What we have learned

  1. Costs decide almost everything.Buying at the ask and selling at the bid costs 2–10% of an option’s price per round trip, more than most daily signals are worth.
  2. Beat “always long”, not zero.Markets mostly rose in 2016–2025, so many models looked good just by being long.
  3. Profits so far ride the market’s drift.Every profitable buyer-side model loses in the same falls (2018, 2022).
  4. Bigger models are not better here.Transformers and neural nets overfit or learned to stay out; the simple linear model is still the benchmark.
  5. Week-by-week market timing is noise.Learned on/off switches stayed out too often and missed rallies (Experiment 7).
  6. Intraday trading lost the most.Paying the spread every hour wipes out any edge (Experiment 2).
  7. Public stock signals show no skillon large, liquid US stocks in 2021–2025 (Experiment 6).
  8. Check the data before believing a result.A stock-split mismatch once produced a fake profit; every dataset now gets a call–put consistency check.
  9. Picking the top-rated of many noisy options picks the riskiest.Forecasts must be shrunk or the menu kept small (Experiment 8).
  10. Selling options diversifies.Put spreads move independently of the benchmark, but weekly premium barely covers costs; monthly does better.
  11. Change the view, not just the model.The first milestone came from trading monthly and combining unrelated edges (Experiment 9), not from a bigger model.
  12. Monthly stock calls mostly deliver leveraged market drift.LeverSet made +11.9% per trade on intraday quotes, but random stocks made +4% and a simple momentum rule beat the transformer (Experiment 17b).
  13. Weekly multi-leg trades drown in costs.Hedged straddles and butterflies lost money at real quotes in every year (Experiment 17c); the daily version only looked break-even because its exits came from a model.
  14. Price every exit.Experiment 16 looked brilliant (Sharpe 2.6) until we found that trades with a missing closing price had been skipped. With every exit priced (Experiment 18) its +28.6% per trade fell to +3.1% and Sharpe to 0.35.
  15. Freeze the design before trusting a result.SetLift’s gains vanished when its hold period was fixed in advance (Experiment 15: 6 of 9 runs positive, needed 7).
  16. Use the longest history available.Momentum calls looked strong on 2022–2025 but earned about nothing over 2016–2025 (Experiment 17a).
  17. Ranking beats regression for picking trades— but no ranker has passed on unbiased data (Experiments 12, 16, 18 and 19).
  18. The put spread survives real quotes; the daily Elastic Net does not.Re-run on 2 PM intraday prices (Experiment 20a), the monthly put spread still earned +8.2% of its maximum loss per trade with 74% winners, while the Elastic Net leg lost 2.2% per trade and sank the combined account.
  19. Check what the data actually contains.DoltHub’s daily files list only three expiries per stock per day, so most 5-day exits had no quote and had to be estimated (Experiment 22); the graph networks still ranked better than the plain ranker, but the result rests on those estimates.
  20. Slow trades survive real quotes; one-day trades do not.All five Top 10 put-spread accounts failed on 2 PM intraday prices because their one-day Elastic Net leg lost money, while every monthly spread part stayed profitable (Experiment 20).
  21. A small learned gate can help a steady spread.On real quotes, a transformer that skips some months lifted the 0.25-delta spread to a daily-return range clearly above zero, a −18% worst drop and losing years of only −7%, −4% and −1% (Experiment 20c).
  22. Further out of the money is steadier.The 0.25-delta put spread earned less than the charter spread on real quotes but was up in 101 of 120 months with a worst drop of only −24% (Experiment 20b) — the steadiest book so far.
  23. A result that flips on a rerun is noise.The same ranker earned +3.1% per trade in Experiment 18 and −5.5% in Experiment 19 with almost identical data; a graph network over related stocks ranked better but still had only one good year in four.
  24. Steady growth is now a goal.Every model is also judged on months up and losing years; the steadiest so far (Experiment 9, 89 of 120 months up) still had two losing years.
  25. Big positions punish volatility.At 5% per position, steady strategies (Experiment 9) grow ~10× faster, but strategies that win only one trade in three are wiped out by losing streaks.
  26. The risk limits are tight on purpose.Even with up to 50% of the account at risk (charter v1.9), +5% a day would need about +10% a day on the money at risk; the ladder tracks realistic progress.
  27. Check that an option can be priced again later.Saved DoltHub data quotes the same option five snapshots later only 2–42% of the time, so exits had to be estimated; the saved SPY/QQQ/IWM file always can — coverage, not price accuracy, decides whether a dataset can test exits.
  28. Cross-check every dataset against an official series.Comparing 30-day implied volatility with the Cboe VIX exposed broken values (SPY file 2008–09, DoltHub November 2021) that summary statistics hid.
  29. Test the same strategy on two data sources.Experiment 9 (end-of-day) and 20a (2 PM quotes): the monthly put spread agreed closely (month-by-month correlation 0.95), but the one-day Elastic Net earned +0.6% a trade at the close and lost 2.2% at 2 PM — a timing-sensitive model.
  30. Choose the number of underlyings on purpose.Three index funds are cheap, steady and well tested but give few trades tied to the market; 24 stocks add stock-picking at higher cost and risk; 100+ stocks add choice but also lucky results and heavy computing (see the Data section).
  31. Graphs help only against random picks.On real 2 PM quotes the option-chain graph beat random options but not a plain ranker, and its daily promise (Experiment 22) did not survive real exits (Experiment 21).
  32. A small edge does not survive big positions.Redone on the saved file for 2014–2025 at 5% per position, the Elastic Net benchmark kept +0.7% per trade but ended at $10,137: one bad year (−63% in 2022) erased the gains (Experiment 1-F).
  33. Long computer jobs must save as they go.A two-hour model run was stopped by the computing time limit minutes before it finished and lost everything; every long run now saves after each test year and resumes from there.
  34. A weak symbol can drag a good model down.With IWM removed, the same Elastic Net went from $10,137 to $22,933 (Sharpe 0.23 → 0.37, 2022 −63% → −9%): IWM trades lost on average while SPY and QQQ made about +1.3% per trade. Check results per symbol before pooling.
  35. The monthly put spread holds up on the standard.On the saved SPY/QQQ file the monthly charter spread made $34,602 alone (Sharpe 0.80) and $79,167 with the Elastic Net (Sharpe 0.67), both with a daily-return range above zero. The standard roughly halves the earlier Sharpe but keeps the edge.
  36. Learning when to sell premium did not beat always selling it.The learning gates were on almost every month, SideFormer chose put spreads most months, and the weekly learners lost; always-on is the honest benchmark for premium models.
  37. Weekly spreads and weekly volatility trades lose to costs.The weekly put spread ended flat and every straddle/butterfly design lost after costs and hedging; holding a month to expiry keeps more of the premium.
  38. More training history is not always better.Starting the daily Elastic Net’s training in 2010 (SPY) and 2012 (QQQ) instead of 2008 raised it from $22,933 to $35,332 (Sharpe 0.37 → 0.50) on the same 2014–2025 test and closed the gap to the original Experiment 1. The 2008–09 crash taught patterns that did not return.
  39. A better benchmark lifts every account built on it.With the v1.3 Elastic Net, charter spread + Elastic Net rose from $79,167 to $122,004 (Sharpe 0.79) while every rule alone stayed the same. The trend-rule account still fails: combining accounts adds growth but can deepen the worst year.
  40. A forecaster no sharper than simple history is worth nothing.On the standard, the DistFormer transformer ($1,832) and a linear quantile model ($5,094) did worse than trading on plain return quantiles ($12,489), and all lost 65–79% in 2022.
  41. A longer hold can look like skill when it is mostly market exposure.Holding the Elastic Net’s calls 5 days made $78,550, but always buying a call and holding 5 days made $59,524, and both lost about 70% in 2022.
  42. A growth objective with a cash option still says “do not trade”.The full ChainFormer chose cash every day on the standard, as it did before.
  43. A switch that is off most of the time can only win by luck.The learned weekly switch was on 9–11% of weeks and made $11,008 against $41,779 always on; the one that edged ahead did it in two early years only.
  44. The time of day matters far more for a 1-day trade than a 5-day trade.On real quotes at 12:00 PM the 1-day Elastic Net made $15,094 (saved file at the 4 PM close: $35,332), while the 5-day hold made $89,478 — at or above its saved-file result.
  45. The last quote of the day is not the closing price.At QuantConnect’s 4:00 PM bar the 1-day Elastic Net turned $10,000 into $1,455 (saved file at the close: $35,332; 12 PM: $15,094), while the 5-day holds and the monthly spreads held up.
  46. A lucky switch does not repeat on a second data source.The weekly logistic switch made $43,702 on the saved file (almost all in 2014 and 2016) but $4,679 at 12 PM and $9,303 at 4 PM on QuantConnect; running both inputs every week held up at noon ($26,464) yet still lost over 80% in 2015 and 2022.
  47. Learning when to sell can cost more than it saves on a rising market.A learned exit held calls about 6 days and made $44,120; holding the same calls 10 trading days made $180,187 (Sharpe 0.85).
  48. An online allocator still pays to learn that a sleeve is bad.Growth-optimal online weights over six sleeves ended at $4,009 because the put sleeves (which lose almost everything) kept coming back.
  49. Check every rule against its start date, and judge leverage by the drop you can survive.The Top 10 #1 call hold was the best of ten start dates (median $99,570); laddering it at 40–50% of equity made millions on paper with drops of 96–98%.
  50. Protections that react to past losses cut the red year but give up the green ones.A 200-day switch to puts turned 2022 from −47% into −3% but lost 49% in 2015; portfolio insurance locked into cash or deepened the worst drop.
  51. Average a rule over its start dates before ranking it.The 10-day call hold averaged over its ten start dates made $208,081 (Sharpe 1.72), more than the single-start median ($99,570).
  52. The drift strategy’s profit is in the upside tail.A call spread, a put-protected call and a seagull cut 2022 but made $19,282, $8,890 and $840 against $198,350 for the plain call.
  53. Option-market fear marks rebounds, not falls.Calls bought on the most stressed days earned +19.7% per 10-day trade, the most of any group; 2022’s slow decline never looked stressed.
  54. Turn a failed warning signal around before discarding it.On 2011–2013, calls bought on the most fearful days earned +36.8% per 10-day trade vs +3.8% on calm days; tilting the ladder toward them made $594,316 with 2022 at −29% instead of −47%.
  55. Pair a lumpy edge with a steady one that earns when the first pays.Adding monthly put spreads to the fear-tilted calls raised months up from 93 to 98 of 144 and growth from $594,316 to $1.94 million.
  56. Stacking short-premium layers adds positive months but fattens the shared tail.A third put-spread layer raised months up to 103 of 144 and growth to $2.90 million, but the worst month deepened to −49% and Sharpe fell.
  57. Waiting for confirmation gives the fear edge away.Calls bought while VIX was still rising earned more (+36.4% on 2011–2013) than on the first day VIX fell (+24.4%).
  58. The later entries in a panic are the ones that catch the rebound.Capping open fear calls softened the worst month but cut growth to $0.4–1.1 million and made 2022 worse.
  59. Four bid–ask crossings per round trip can be bigger than the edge.Long call calendars lost 11% per 10-day trade and reverse calendars 4% on SPY/QQQ after costs.
  60. Hysteresis stops chatter around a line, not false breaks.A Schmitt-trigger switch removed only 7 of 54 downtrend call spreads; the 2015–2016 falls looked like 2022 at first.
  61. Check how often a signal fires before testing it.A Fed-tightening signal fires only in 2022–2023 in the saved data, so a test would just fit 2022; it was not run (Experiment 36).
  62. An outside signal can separate red years that look alike inside option prices.A Fed-tightening switch cut 2022 from −34% to −10%, left 2015 alone and kept growth ($2.82 million).
  63. A sequence transformer cannot learn regimes from a few hundred independent episodes.It had no ranking skill and was most optimistic in 2022; the one-line fear rule beat it.
  64. A published calendar anomaly need not survive in option returns.Calls bought at the turn of the month earned less on 2011–2013; adding exposure there cut positive months.
  65. Not every macro series separates the red years.Free FRED data: credit spreads widened more in 2015 than in 2022, and the yield curve stayed inverted through the strong years 2023–2024; only the Fed-tightening signal fired in 2022 and stayed off in 2015.
  66. The volatility of VIX picks panic rebounds better than VIX levels or skew.Top-fifth VVIX days earned +56% per call on never-traded 2011–2013 (old fear score +45%); VVIX alone made $10.6 million at Sharpe 2.10.
  67. Keep selling premium in macro stress.Put spreads sold after fast moves in the dollar, NFCI, 2-year yield or oil earned more on never-traded 2011–2013 (+12.2% vs +2.5%).
  68. Don’t buy short-dated calls right before scheduled news.Calls entered the day before or of FOMC/CPI earned +6.9% vs +15.6% (2011–13); skipping them gave 108/144 positive months at $2.83 million.
  69. A filter is free only when the trades it removes are near break-even.Skipping calls before FOMC/CPI cost nothing on Top 10 #1 (+2% trades) but $3 million on VVIX alone (+12% trades), for 5 more positive months.
  70. You cannot bank green months that never turn green.Only 3 of 44 red months ever reached +5% first; 14 were near-misses where small calm-day calls bled while the spreads earned.
  71. The small calm-day calls drive the red months and the 2022 loss.Dropping them gave 106/144 positive months, 9 S1 years and 2022 +6%; keeping them and adding a third put-spread layer gave $15.3 million.
  72. Without the calm-day calls, the S1 blocker moves to the premium layers.4 of 5 red 2022 months had no fear call open; the spreads lost in the slow bear market, so call filters left 106/144 months and 9 S1 years.
  73. Whether a guard helps depends on the other layers.No new put spreads in a Fed-tightening downtrend hurt the account with calm-day calls but gave the fearful-days-only account its first 10 S1 years (108/144 months, 2022 +18%).
  74. Neither green-month probability nor Kelly growth alone fits the goal.Probability-max gave 123/144 positive months but $12,079; Kelly gave $1.53 billion on paper with a −77% drop and broke the 50% cap.
  75. A hand-built account beats walk-forward optimisation over the same layers.Under a 75% floor and the 50% cap the optimiser matched Top 10 #5 on months and S1 years but made $313,258 vs $5.04 million.
  76. Negative VRP and shock clustering warn about open positions, not new spreads.Spreads sold after shocks earned the most on 2011–2013 (+10.1% vs +2.1%); skipping them cut Top 10 #5 to 90–103 positive months.
  77. A robust ranking is not a proven Sharpe level.Overfitting probability was low (0.03), but no Top 10 account reached a deflated Sharpe of 0.95; expect live results well below the back-tests.
  78. A drawdown bound on the mix starves the income layers.Risk-constrained Kelly cut the put spreads and gave 94/144 positive months; plain Kelly with a daily 50% cap made $18.1 million with a −67% drop.
  79. The Hurst regime adds almost nothing beyond the trend and the Fed signal.SPY’s daily returns are mildly anti-persistent (H ≈ 0.44); the rule changed only 2–10 trades on Top 10 #6, all wrongly.
  80. A log-periodic bubble flag did not warn before our falls.Falls of 10% or more were less likely after a flag than after an average week; the 2015, 2018 and 2020 shocks came unflagged.
  81. Taking profit early on short spreads trades income for win rate.Closing at 50% of the credit raised winners from 84% to 90% but cut the mean per spread from 7.6% to 4.8%; positive months fell to 103/144.
  82. Blending averages returns, not signs.An online blend of Top 10 #2 and #6 had 103/144 positive months, fewer than either alone; with correlated accounts the learned weights barely moved.
  83. Risk parity discards an edge that sits where the risk is.Hierarchical risk parity cut the VVIX fear calls to 6–13% of their size; the account ended at $53,671 despite a −35% worst drop.
  84. The saved file is a faithful stand-in for real quotes.Every layer matched on QuantConnect (monthly correlation 0.87–0.995); fixed-rule #2 and #6 kept 93% and 86% of their growth.
  85. Optimised weights do not survive a change of data source.The Kelly-weighted #1 fell from $12.3 million to $191,155 on real quotes; fixed rules held.
  86. Full-Kelly size is fragile to a small loss of edge.50-Q K failed mainly because it runs the fear calls at double size; on real quotes their edge fell from +23.8% to +20.8% a trade, and growth fell far more. Fixed-size #2 and #6 lost only 7–14% of their growth.
  87. Run QuantConnect tests the practical way.Subscribe only the contracts a rule needs (the full 2012–2025 run took 15 minutes), subscribe an hour before the decision, build the calendar from price bars, log compact summaries, and verify one shared accounting module first.
  88. Every fixed-rule account in the Top 6 survives real quotes.39-Q B, 36-Q A and 41-Q A kept 87–91% of their daily growth; VVIX alone kept a Sharpe of 2.00. Expect about half the saved end value.
  89. All eight fixed-rule accounts in the Top 9 survive real quotes.43-Q D, 31-Q A and 30-Q B kept 87–88% of their daily growth; across all eight, 86–93% kept and Sharpe only 0.04–0.18 lower. Rank by real-quote Sharpe and positive months, not saved end value.

Full record of every model’s pros, cons and lesson (126 lessons): docs/LESSONS_LEARNED_MODELS.md in the project repository.

How we test

Two paths, the same five steps

StepPath A: original designPath B: build on existing models
1. Define successNet account return per day after all costs, on years the model never saw; beat simple rules and Elastic Net; stay inside the risk limits
2. BaselineSimple rules, a linear model, gradient boosting and a small standard networkThe same, plus published strategies rebuilt on our data
3. HypothesisA new mechanism aimed at a failure we saw, written down before testingA combination of strengths that should work together
4. Test one changeEach mechanism on and off (ablations)Each borrowed part on and off; vs its sources
5. Refine or change viewKeep what holds across seeds and years; after rounds without progress, change the trade type, horizon or instruments

Unseen years

Models are retrained every year on earlier data only and judged on the following year (walk-forward). Sealed periods are opened once, for frozen models.

Honest costs

Buy at the ask, sell at the bid, plus $0.65 per contract; every result rerun at +25% and +50% wider spreads.

Fair tests

A written plan before each run, 3 random seeds for neural models, a data check on every new dataset, and every result kept, including failures.

Next

Experiment 20 is complete. None of the five Top 10 put-spread + Elastic Net accounts survives real intraday quotes (the Elastic Net leg fails); every spread part does, and the gated 0.25-delta put spread is the best and steadiest. Experiment 21 (a graph network over each option chain on intraday quotes) is done: no pass. Experiment 22 (both graph networks on daily data) is done: no pass. Next: group every experiment into strategy families, then redo all experiments on the saved SPY/QQQ/IWM file (see below).

Data rule (Nov 9, 2026): from now on, daily models use only the SPY/QQQ/IWM end-of-day file (full option chains, 2008–2025), which a cross-check against three other sources and the VIX showed is trustworthy. DoltHub is no longer used. To redo later: every experiment that used DoltHub — Experiments 5, 6, 10, 12, 13 and 22, the stock parts of 14 and 15, and the DoltHub-based 2026 checks of Experiments 1 and 9 — will be re-run on the SPY/QQQ/IWM file. Until then their results are marked as weaker.

After Experiment 21: one fixed test setup for every model (Nov 9, 2026). So that models and experiments can be compared fairly, only the model will change:

  • QuantConnect standard test: the same instruments (SPY and QQQ only — IWM dropped on Nov 9; the 24-stock list deferred), the same test years (2014–2025; no 2026 check — owner, Nov 10), training from 2012 for both SPY and QQQ (QuantConnect’s option data starts in January 2012 — a data limit; the saved file trains SPY from 2010), one decision a day at 12 PM ET plus a run on the last hourly quote of the day (the 4:00 PM bar), closest to the saved file’s 4 PM close (a 3:45 PM run needs minute quotes, about 40 hours on the free plan), buy at the ask and sell at the bid with fees, every exit at a real quote, $10,000 with 5% per position, and the same benchmarks in every run.
  • Daily models: only the saved SPY/QQQ/IWM file.
  • SPY and QQQ only (Nov 9, 2026): both sources now trade and learn from SPY and QQQ only. In the first redo the Elastic Net lost 1.2% a trade on IWM while making about +1.5% on SPY and QQQ, so IWM is dropped and every redo runs again on SPY/QQQ.
  • Test window (Nov 9, 2026): every model is tested on 2014–2025 on both sources, the saved file and QuantConnect, so all are compared on the same 12 years. Learning models train on the years before each test year.
  • Training start (Nov 9, 2026): on both sources, learning models train only on SPY data from 2010 and QQQ data from 2012, as Experiment 1 did. Training SPY from 2008 (the 2008–09 crisis) gave a weaker Elastic Net than Experiment 1, so every redo runs again with this start; the runs trained from 2008 stay as records.
  • Cross-check: index models run on both sources. Similar results mean a robust model; a big gap means it depends on the exact trading time (like the 1-day Elastic Net: +0.6% a trade daily, −2.2% at 2 PM).
  • Order: (1) redo on the saved SPY/QQQ/IWM file every experiment that didn’t use it — the DoltHub experiments and the QuantConnect experiments (2, 16–21); with only SPY and QQQ, the many-stock families C (stock call picking) and E (graph networks) and Exp. 10 are not redone (owner, Nov 10; they stay as pre-standard records) → (2) rank every model on that one file and pick the new Top 10 → (3) run only those Top 10 on the QuantConnect standard test. Older results stay, marked “pre-standard”.

Down markets (Nov 9, 2026). Our best strategies win when the market rises or stays calm and lose in declines: in 2022 the put spread lost 17% (end-of-day) to 42% (2 PM quotes) and momentum calls 44–87%. From the redo on, every model must also handle falls:

  • Judge the downside: every model reports its worst year and its results in 2018, 2020 and 2022.
  • Test 2014–2025 on both sources (2018, 2020 and 2022 are the declines in the window); models still learn from 2008 onward, including the 2008 crash.
  • Standard market gate: the 200-day trend plus the VIX term structure (short-term fear above 3-month fear); every model tested with and without it.
  • Protection over prediction: call spreads, cash or a cheap put hedge in downtrends, rather than trying to time the fall exactly.
  • Profit from falls (two-way design): predict up / down / unclear and pick the trade — sell a put spread, sell a call spread or buy a put spread, or stay in cash. The Experiment 11 trend rule already did this: +53% in 2022 with Elastic Net, but false signals cost it in choppy years (2016 −8%, 2023 −24%).

Same scale on every chart, so they can be compared at a glance. Dashed line: start of the sealed 2024–2025 test, run only for the models carried forward. Verdict: the best daily benchmark so far, but not yet proven. Elastic Net turned $10,000 into $35,332 over 2014–2025 (Sharpe 0.50, +1.75% per trade, worst drop -64%, +2% in 2022). Its daily-return range still includes zero and one year (2024, +86%) carries much of the gain. It defines L0 for the saved-file Top 10.

What it shows. It buys calls only, split between SPY (1,085 trades, +1.65% each) and QQQ (974, +1.85%), and stays in cash all of 2023 (no positive score). It had no loss in the three down years (2018, 2020, 2022). The market gate makes it worse ($10,930) by skipping rebound days. Every other model and rule loses nearly everything, including the shuffled-label control.

Why the training start matters. The same model trained from 2008 ended at $22,933 (Sharpe 0.37). Dropping the 2008–09 crash years from training lifted it to $35,332, and on 2016–2025 it now gives $51,862 against $51,946 for the original Experiment 1 — the gap to the original is closed. That run is kept as a record in results/EXP01F_SPYQQQ_RESULTS_2026-11-09.md.

Record: the SPY/QQQ/IWM run (superseded). The same test with IWM included ended at $10,137 (Sharpe 0.23, worst drop −80%, −63% in 2022); IWM trades lost on average. That result led to the SPY/QQQ-only decision and is kept in results/EXP01F_RESULTS_2026-11-09.md.

Verdict: a 5-day hold reaches L1 on growth, but mostly by holding calls longer in a rising market.

Holding the Elastic Net’s picks for 5 days turned $10,000 into $78,550 (Sharpe 0.58, +6.4% per trade) with a daily-return range above zero. But simply buying a call every day and holding 5 days made $59,524, and both lost about 70% in 2022 — far worse than the 1-day Elastic Net’s worst year (−40%). The 3-day hold made $43,318; the 2-day hold only $16,291. The gate hurts every hold, and gradient boosting and the momentum rule lose at every hold. (The 1-day row books returns on the exit day, so it shows $35,308 against 1-F’s $35,332; the trades are the same.)

Saved-file Top 10 check: the 5-day hold is an L1 candidate with the 2022 caveat; it must beat always-call 5-day in the QuantConnect test. Full table: results/EXP01D2F_V13_RESULTS_2026-11-10.md.

Result: no model works intraday

  • Every model and rule lost money after the bid/ask spread and fees, in every year.
  • The cost of a one-hour round trip (about 1.3–1.7% of the option price) is bigger than what an hour of price movement earns. Simple rules lost 79–87% of the account.
  • The models mostly learned not to trade — the best they could do was lose slowly.
  • Sealed 2024–Aug 2026 test (opened once, best simple rule only): always buying a call lost 0.85% per trade over 7,711 trades ($10,000 → $377) — confirming the result.

Result: no improvement on Elastic Net

  • The full model refused to trade — trained to grow the account with realistic costs, it judged every option trade not worth the spread.
  • The simpler version without attention made a little ($14,274 over 2016–2025), mostly with 3–5-day call holds.
  • Elastic Net stays the best model ($51,946). Lesson: the edge must come from forecasting the market itself — the idea behind the next model, DistFormer (running now).

Experiment 4: DistFormer — charts and result

Experiment 4 — new model: DistFormer (forecast the market, then price real options)

Built Nov 7, 2026. Step 1: forecast the full range of SPY/QQQ moves over the next 1–5 days. Step 2 (no learning): reprice every real option in 256 scenarios using its actual bid/ask, with costs 25% above real, and buy only where the expected profit is positive. Three versions show which step matters. Retrained every year, tested 2016–2025.

No-skill distribution

Made money

Prices every real option against how much SPY/QQQ have historically moved, buys where it is cheap (mostly 5-day calls). Best new model so far.

$10,000 → (2016–2025)

Linear forecaster

Made a little

A simple linear model forecasts the range of moves; same option pricing step.

$10,000 → (2016–2025)

Transformer forecaster (DistFormer)

Lost a little

A transformer reads 60 days of market history to forecast the range of moves. Added nothing.

$10,000 → (2016–2025)

Result: the pricing step helps, the forecasting doesn’t

  • Best new model so far: the no-skill version turned $10,000 into $18,744 (2016–2025), +8.3% per trade — more money than Elastic Net ($51,946), but with bigger swings (Sharpe 0.52 vs 0.68–0.73), so it does not yet clear the first progress step.
  • The transformer forecaster added nothing — SPY/QQQ direction is too hard to forecast from past data.
  • Next: change perspective — single-stock options across ~140 companies, with market direction hedged out, where published research finds lasting edges.

Experiment 5: VolSet (140 stocks) — charts and result

Experiment 5 — new perspective: VolSet (about 140 individual stocks, weekly volatility trades)

Built Nov 7, 2026 after two rounds on SPY/QQQ without progress. Instead of betting on direction, each trade bets on how much a stock will move: buy a straddle when moves look underpriced, or sell a protected iron butterfly when they look overpriced, with the stock’s direction hedged out daily. Up to 10 positions a week, each risking at most 5% of the account. Tested 2022–2025.

Gradient-boosted trees choosing which stocks to trade each week. Broke even.

Always sell butterflies

$10,000 → (2022–2025)

Goyal–Saretto rule

Classic research rule: buy volatility where it looks cheap, sell where expensive.

$10,000 → (2022–2025)

Result: no progress — and a false alarm caught

  • The first run looked like a breakthrough ($10,000 → $20,530). Our checks traced it to a data error: stock prices were adjusted for splits but option strikes were not. Fixed and rerun with the same models: the gains disappeared.
  • After the fix, nothing makes money: the best model broke even; selling options every week lost half the account. Single-stock option spreads (3–4% per leg) are too costly for weekly trading.
  • Next perspective: use options where they are cheapest — deep in-the-money calls as low-cost leverage on slow, well-documented stock signals, held for a month.

Ten positions, each risking at most 5% of the account. Tested 2021–2025.

Result: no progress — the gains are just the market

  • Best version: $10,000 → $8,157 (2021–2025), but with big swings (Sharpe 0.44) and a loss in 2022.
  • No stock-picking skill: the rankings had essentially zero correlation with next month’s returns. After removing the market’s own move, every version lost money.
  • What four rounds show: every positive result so far comes from the market’s upward drift and fails in the same market falls. Next perspective: combine those strategies and learn when to be invested.
Experiment 7: RegimeGate (when to be invested) — charts and result

Experiment 7 — new perspective: RegimeGate (learn when to be invested)

Built Nov 7, 2026. Every strategy that made money so far rode the market’s upward drift and lost in the same falls (2022). Instead of a new edge, this round combines the two best out-of-sample strategies (Elastic Net 1-day calls and DistFormer 3–5-day calls) and decides each week whether each one should trade. Tested 2018–2025.

Both strategies, always on

Made money

No timing at all. Most money of any model so far, but bigger swings and still a loss in 2022.

$10,000 → (2018–2025)

Trend + volatility rule

Made money

Trade only when SPY is above its 200-day average and short-term fear (VIX) is below 3-month fear.

$10,000 → (2018–2025)

Elastic Net alone (benchmark)

Best quality

The model every new one must beat. Smoothest ride of the round (Sharpe 0.77).

$10,000 → (2018–2025)

Logistic gate

Made a little

Simple learned on/off switch from last week’s market state.

$10,000 → (2018–2025)

RegimeGate (transformer)

Made a little

Reads 26 weeks of market history and switches each strategy on or off. Too cautious: on only 37% / 6% of weeks.

$10,000 → (2018–2025)

Result: no progress — timing the market week by week doesn’t help

  • No on/off switch beat Elastic Net alone on quality (Sharpe 0.77). The learned switches stayed out too often and missed rallies; the transformer was the most cautious and did worst ($13,067).
  • Running both strategies all the time made the most money ($10,000 → $40,402) but with bigger drops: both lose in the same weeks.
  • What five rounds show: as option buyers we pay the bid/ask spread twice and depend on the market rising. Next perspective (Experiment 8): be the option seller — collect insurance premium on SPY/QQQ with loss-capped put spreads held to expiry, which held up in 2020 and 2022.

Experiment 8 — new perspective: PremiumSet (be the option seller)

Built Nov 7, 2026. Instead of buying options, sell weekly loss-capped put and call spreads on SPY, QQQ and IWM and hold them to expiry, so the bid/ask spread is paid once. A set transformer looks at about 100 possible spreads each week and picks which to sell, or stays in cash. Each position risks at most 5% of the account. Tested 2016–2025.

Result: no progress — selling premium weekly is about break-even after costs

  • The classic weekly put spread made $10,000 → $9,813 in ten years: the insurance premium collected is about the size of the bid/ask spread paid.
  • The transformer lost most of its stake ($0): its forecasts had no skill, and always picking the top-rated of ~100 candidates picked the riskiest ones.
  • Good news: the put spread moves independently of Elastic Net (correlation −0.01), so together they earned more than Elastic Net alone — but not yet with a better risk-adjusted return.

Experiment 9: MonthlyPremium (monthly put spreads + Elastic Net) — charts and result

Experiment 9 — MonthlyPremium: sell premium monthly, combined with Elastic Net

Built Nov 7, 2026. Lesson from Experiment 8: weekly premium barely covers costs. So sell put spreads on SPY, QQQ and IWM once a month (the spread is paid 4× less often), keep the choice fixed, and run them in the same account as Elastic Net. A small transformer only decides whether to sell each month. Each spread risks at most 5% of the account. Tested 2016–2025, then checked on fresh 2026 data.

Charter put spread + Elastic Net

Passed L0

Short a near-the-money put, buy one 5% lower, every month; plus the benchmark. Sharpe 1.04 vs 0.68.

A safer, further-out spread plus the benchmark. Sharpe 0.91.

Benchmark

Charter put spread alone

Made money

The spreads on their own: steady, and unrelated to the benchmark’s ups and downs.

$10,000 → (2016–2025)

Result: first milestone (L0) passed in the development test

  • $10,000 → $203,352 (2016–2025) with the charter spread + Elastic Net at 5% per position: about +0.12% a day (L2 level), Sharpe 1.04 against 0.68 for Elastic Net alone, but a worst drop of about −53%; still positive with 25% higher costs. (At the original 0.5% sizing: $14,550, worst drop −6.8%.)
  • Why it works: Elastic Net earns in rallies, the put spreads in calm or slowly rising markets, so their ups and downs don’t line up (correlation ≈ 0).
  • Fresh-data check (Dec 2025 – Oct 2026, SPY): the spreads stayed profitable — +8.8% and +11.8% of their maximum risk per trade, 9 and 7 of 10 months positive. Elastic Net can’t be re-tested on 2026 yet, so L0 is reached in development and supported, not yet confirmed.
  • Honest caveats: the gain came from the change of perspective, not the new model; the spread design was seen before in a benchmark; and the higher daily return at 5% comes from larger positions, not a better edge — with drops of about half the account.

Experiment 12: rebuilding the reference system on single-stock options — charts and result

Experiment 12 — the reference system, rebuilt faithfully (single-stock options)

Built Nov 7–8, 2026 at the owner’s request. A fresh review of the reference screenshots showed it trades single-stock options (NOW, PLTR, AAPL, MSFT…), holds for days, and picks only top-ranked contracts. We rebuilt it on 1.6 million real option quotes for 134 large stocks (2020–2026): the same 5×200 network, a version tuned for rare big winners, and a new set-transformer successor. Tested 2022–2025, then on sealed Jan–Oct 2026 data. Ten positions at a time, 5% of the account each. Dashed line: start of 2024 (and the 2026 test follows Dec 2025).

SetLift (new set transformer)

Result: the pattern is reproducible; the profit isn’t reliable yet

  • Correction on the reference: its 7.7% is the total gain on premium for a week of new positions, not a daily account return; most of its 10-day profit came from one day’s entries.
  • The fat right tail is real and reproducible: our tail model’s typical trade lost 30%, but 1 in 100 trades gained over 300% (best +2,993%). On average, though, the winners did not cover the losers in 2022–2025.
  • SetLift on unseen 2026 data: made +16.6% per trade (Sharpe 1.53; $10,000 → $13,850 at the original 0.5% sizing), but at 5% per position its large swings turn that into a loss ($10,000 → $5,737), and it lost in 3 of 4 earlier years — not robust. In the reference’s own Aug 17–27 window it lost.
  • Main obstacle: single-stock option spreads average about 13% of the price; buying an average contract and selling it later loses about 10%.

Why it is provisional. For 22% of candidates the exit price was missing (the contract left QuantConnect’s strike window after a big move, or had no bid). The simulation skipped those and took the next-best pick — information not available on the entry day. Many of the skipped contracts are likely near-worthless losers, so the result is biased upward by an unknown amount. If every skipped exit had been a total loss, LiftRank’s average trade would fall from +28.6% to roughly 0%.

What it shows anyway. On the same data, ranking (LiftRank) beat regression, both beat random picks by over 20 points per trade, and the reference network stayed near zero. Next (owner decision): re-run with missing exits priced conservatively (no bid → worth $0; out of window → intrinsic value), before any 2026 holdout.

Verdict: no pass. LiftRank earned +3.1% per trade and was positive in all four years, and it beat random picks and the momentum rule — but its daily-return range includes zero and its Sharpe is 0.35 against the 1.04 needed. The sealed 2026 data stays sealed.

What it shows. Experiment 16’s spectacular result came almost entirely from skipping trades whose exit price was missing — usually the ones that had collapsed. Honest exits leave a small edge with a median trade of −9%, so at 5% per position the frequent total losses outweigh the winners (19 of 48 months up). Ranking still ordered the models the same way: ranker > momentum > regression > random > reference network.

Experiment 19: StockGraph, a graph neural network over related stocks, 2022–2025 — charts and result

Experiment 19 — StockGraph: graph attention over related stocks

Run Nov 9, 2026 on QuantConnect, on exactly the setup of Experiment 18 (24 large stocks, calls and puts 20–45 days out, bought at the ask at 2 PM ET, sold at the bid 5 trading days later, top 5 a day when SPY is above its 200-day average, every exit priced, models retrained each year). Each day the stocks form a graph: links between stocks in the same sector, to each stock’s 3 most correlated stocks over 60 days, and to the market (SPY). A two-layer graph attention network learns a summary of each stock from its neighbours; combined with each option’s own features it ranks the day’s options. Compared with the same ranker given simple neighbour averages, the plain ranker and random picks. 5% of the account per position.

The plain ranker, run again with identical code on almost identical data, went from +3.1% per trade (Experiment 18) to −5.5%: its earlier result was luck. The next step returns to loss-capped spreads, the one family that has worked on daily data (Experiment 20).

Experiment 21 — ChainGraph on real 2 PM quotes

Run Nov 9, 2026 on QuantConnect’s hourly option quotes for the 24 large stocks (AAPL, MSFT, NVDA, AMZN, META, GOOGL, TSLA, AMD, AVGO, NFLX, NOW, CRM, ORCL, ADBE, INTU, MU, QCOM, JPM, UNH, LLY, COST, XOM, BA, PLTR), as planned and frozen beforehand. Experiment 23: StopLearner — learned optimal stopping on the saved SPY/QQQ file, 2014–2025 — charts and result

Experiment 23 — learning when to buy and when to sell

Run Nov 10, 2026 on the saved SPY/QQQ file under the standard (v1.3). Every experiment so far sold on a fixed rule. Here the model learns when to get out, using the method banks use to value American options (Longstaff–Schwartz): at each day it compares selling now with the expected value of holding, learned from the real 10-day price paths of earlier trades. Candidates: the ~0.50-delta call and put with 21–35 days to expiry, each day, on SPY and QQQ; bought at the ask, sold at the bid, $0.65 per contract, 5% per position, at most 10 open. Walk-forward: tuned on earlier years, checked on the year before, then traded. Plan written before any result.

The full StopLearner ended at $16,865 (Sharpe 0.29). With the same daily call purchases, the learned exit made $44,120, while simply holding 5 days made $78,281 and holding 10 days made $180,187 (Sharpe 0.85, worst drop −45%). The learned rule sells winners too early (about 6 days on average) and gives up the market’s upward drift.

The 10-day hold is the strongest saved-file result so far, above the Top 10 #1 ($122,004). It is a simple rule found as a comparison, not the planned model, and it is mostly long market exposure: it lost 18% in 2015 and 44% in 2022. Confirmed with a separate calculation. Later finding (Exp. 25): it depends on its start date — $58,450 to $180,187 over the first 10 possible start days, median $99,570.

Top 10 check: the 10-day hold is now #1 on the saved-file Top 10 (owner, Nov 10). Full table: results/EXP23_STOPLEARNER_RESULTS_2026-11-10.md.

Experiment 35: SchmittTrend — a hysteresis switch for the downtrend layer, 2014–2025 — charts and result

Experiment 35 — borrowing the Schmitt trigger from electronics

Run Nov 10, 2026 on the saved SPY/QQQ file (standard v1.3). The trend rule’s call spreads (sold below the 200-day average) cut 2022 to −6% when added to the Top 10 #1, but whipsaws in 2015–2016 cost more. Verdict: the ranking is robust, the Sharpe level is not proven.

Probability of backtest overfitting: 0.029 (low). Deflated Sharpe: no Top 10 account reaches 0.95 (best 0.27, VVIX alone): with ~240 attempts the best of ~13 unskilled tries would be expected near Sharpe 2.31, and the accounts’ fat left tails widen the doubt. Expect a live Sharpe well below 2; real-quote testing is the true out-of-sample check.

Verdict: the fixed-rule accounts hold up on real quotes; the optimised one does not.

Every layer has almost the same trades, mean return and win rate on QuantConnect as in the saved file (monthly correlation 0.87–0.995). 43-Q E (#2) and 45-Q A (#6) are robust, keeping 93% and 86% of their daily growth with similar Sharpe, positive months and worst drop — their end values are lower ($8.8 million and $2.05 million) because a few percent less daily growth compounds over 12 years. 50-Q K (#1) does not hold up ($191,155): its Kelly weights are re-fitted each year from layer returns, and small differences send the optimiser to a different mix. Time of day matters for the downtrend call spreads (2022: +22% at the close, +25% at 3:45 PM, +10% at 12 PM).

Top 10 check: no change to the saved-file ranking; the QuantConnect results are listed for the owner’s decision. Full table: results/EXP_Q_TOP3_RESULTS_2026-11-11.md.

Buy-and-hold made the most money. Selling options smoothed the ride but gave up most of the gains and still fell about 30% in the worst month; short straddles lost. Our model had the best return per unit of risk, but at the 0.5% risk limit it makes little money. Simulated; not investment advice.

Follow-up tests (Nov 7, 2026)

QuestionAnswer
Is the best model skilled at options, or just at market direction?Market direction. It picks days when SPY/QQQ go on to rise (+0.16% next day vs +0.04% on other days); after removing that move, no extra gain remains.
Do longer holds beat the bid/ask cost?Yes, for every call-buying approach. Holding 5 days: best model +7.9% per trade — but simply always buying a call made +7.4%. The model’s real advantage is a smaller worst drop at a 1-day hold (−4% vs −14%).
What does the model look at?Prefers calls, bought after calm, slightly falling markets: low recent volatility, a small 5-day dip, falling implied volatility, tight spreads.
Does the working system’s network help?No. We rebuilt its network from the screenshots (5 layers × 200 units; gain and tradability outputs; separate calls and puts). On daily data it lost 0.7% per trade at a 1-day hold and made +2.1% at 5 days — below the simple linear model. Its tradability output helped a little.
Does it hold up in 2026?Not enough data to say: only 34–42 trades in the 2026 check.

What this shows

  • Only one model made money: of eight models, only Elastic Net ended above $10,000; LightGBM, the neural network, the rules and a random pick all lost after costs.
  • A small, steady gain at the risk limit: $10,000 → $12,200 over ten years (about 2% a year), while always buying calls fell to $9,030 and the momentum rule to $5,500.
  • Bigger bets help only up to a point: 10% per trade reached $99,640 (about 26% a year) but with a 60% fall along the way; 25% per trade ended at $5,020.
  • Far from the goal: even the best size made about 0.1% a day against the >5%-a-day target.
  • Small accounts can’t follow it: one SPY option costs about $300–800, so with $1,000 a single contract is 30–80% of the account.
  • What the edge is: the model mostly picks days when SPY and QQQ go on to rise; it is market timing expressed through calls, not an options-specific advantage. A rebuilt version of the working system’s network did no better.
How the experiments work

How the experiments work

Narrow on purpose, and fixed before looking at the test period. These are starting assumptions, not settings known to be profitable.

MarketsSPY and QQQ first, then options on the 150 most-traded underlyings
TradesBuy calls or puts; debit spreads as a second test
Expiry7–21 days out, delta 0.35–0.60
TimingDecide every 15 minutes, hold 60 minutes, close same day needs intraday data — daily versions (1–5 day holds) run first
FillsBuy at the ask, sell at the bid, plus fees and delay
TargetProfit per contract after costs, in $ and % of premium

Models, in order

  1. Simple rules and linear model — the baseline every model must beat. tested linear model best so far
  2. LightGBM — first main model. tested lost after costs
  3. Small neural network — with and without a tradability output and call/put outputs. tested below the linear model; tradability output helped a little
  4. LSTM or causal CNN — uses recent market history. next, with intraday data
  5. Later, only if they add profit: transformers, graph models, reinforcement learning.

First results: daily version on SPY and QQQ (Nov 7, 2026)

Intraday option prices aren’t available yet, so the experiment was first run on daily decisions: buy one call or put at the close, sell it at the next day’s close, paying the full bid/ask spread and fees. Rules were written down before any result, models were retrained each year (tested 2016–2023), and 2024–2025 was kept sealed and opened once.

Average net return per trade, 2016–2023 (%)

After the spread and fees. Positive means the model made money per trade.

  • One model shows a possible edge: the linear (Elastic Net) model averaged +2.6% per trade in testing and +2.4% in the sealed 2024–2025 period, though that period alone isn’t statistically conclusive.
  • It works as a timing rule for buying calls: on the days it picks, a plain call earned money; on the days it skips, the same call lost.
  • It is small: at the 0.5%-per-trade risk limit the account grows about 1.5–4% a year. The >5%-a-day goal is far out of reach for this design (it made about 0.01% a day).
  • Everything else — simple rules, LightGBM, a small neural network — lost money after costs. The bid/ask spread is the main hurdle on a one-day hold.

Simulated results on historical data; not investment advice.

Outside models we learn from

Outside models we learn from

A starting list, not a ranking. Each is profiled and run on our task before any of its parts are reused.

Proven on option data

  • Gradient-boosted trees on option features: profitable after costs in a 1996–2020 study (Bali et al.)
  • LSTM with a turnover penalty: kept a Sharpe ratio of 0.69 at 50 bps cost vs 0.39 without (Tan et al.)
  • Tree-based volatility forecasts: 13% lower error on one-month implied volatility (Federal Reserve)
  • Surface and chain models (CNN, graph networks) and deep hedging, for later
  • The reference system: separate “gain” and “tradability” outputs — rebuilt and tested Nov 7 (5×200 network): below the linear model on daily data; the tradability output helped a little

General forecasting models

  • TimesFM-3 (Google, 2026): many series at once, gives ranges not just points; non-commercial checkpoint
  • Chronos-2 (Amazon): uses related series and extra inputs without retraining
  • TiRex 2 (NXAI): compact recurrent forecaster
  • Toto 2 (Datadog): not yet independently checked
  • PatchTST and TFT: proven transformer designs

These forecast prices, not option profit, and finance studies show general benchmark rankings don’t carry over. So each is re-ranked on our own test.

Simulated on historical data; not investment advice.
